title: The East, again
tomorrow: what was a brilliant young man in Milan so restless for?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary at Cana named the need and pointed to her son: do whatever he tells you. Today, a picture about breathing.
screen: `DO WHATEVER HE TELLS YOU.` → `A PICTURE ABOUT BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Swimmers learn to breathe on both sides. Breathe only to one side and you can still swim, but you drift, and you tire sooner. Pope John Paul the Second used a picture like that for the whole Church. In a letter on Christian unity, he wrote that the Church must breathe with her two lungs, the East and the West. So what is the other lung, and what does it breathe?
screen: `SWIMMERS BREATHE ON BOTH SIDES.` → `TWO LUNGS: EAST AND WEST.` → `WHAT IS THE OTHER LUNG?`

segments.voice: The question is: can Christians who pray so differently still belong to one body? The East is the Christianity of Greece, the Middle East, Russia, Ukraine, Egypt, Ethiopia, India and more. Some Eastern Churches are Catholic, in full communion with the pope, with their own liturgies and saints. Here's the one to tell a friend: in Eastern Catholic Churches, married men can be ordained priests, by their own tradition. And then there's the neighbor: the Orthodox Churches. In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, just before the Creed, the deacon calls out, in effect: let us love one another, that with one mind we may confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Love first, then the Creed. Catholics recognize so much shared ground: the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles, Mary honored as Theotokos, the God-bearer, and icons. A council at Nicaea taught that the honor given an icon passes to the one it shows. The difference is honest, too. Catholics and Orthodox aren't in full communion. Orthodox Christians don't accept the pope's authority as Catholics understand it, and that difference is real. Jesus prayed in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Not the same. Not strangers. Two lungs that have learned to breathe in different rhythms.
screen: `EASTERN CATHOLIC CHURCHES.` · `THE ORTHODOX: LOVE, THEN THE CREED.` · `SHARED: SACRAMENTS, THEOTOKOS, ICONS.` · `DIFFERENT: THE POPE'S ROLE.` · then, large: `BOTH LUNGS.`

segments.voice: Find an icon or a holy image, on a wall or a screen; if there isn't one, a photo of someone you love will do. Look at the face, especially the eyes, and breathe slowly, both sides of your chest filling. If you pray, you can pray with the image as Eastern Christians do, letting the honor pass through it to the one it shows.
The East. The Christian traditions of the East, Catholic and Orthodox: one of the Church's two lungs.
Keep this: both lungs, East and West, not the same and not strangers. That's today.

howItsDone: Eastern Catholic Churches celebrate their own liturgies, like the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, in full communion with the pope; Catholics and Orthodox Christians both pray with icons and honor Mary as Theotokos, while working through what still divides them.

fork.setup: your Orthodox friend asks if your churches are basically the same now. what's the fairest answer?
options: close kin: shared sacraments, Mary, icons; not yet one communion, mainly over the pope.
yes, exactly the same; only the language and music are different.
no real connection; the two split apart long ago and share nothing now.
fork.reveal: the shared ground is deep, and the difference is honest. John Paul II's picture: one body that must breathe with both lungs.

chat.says: video call with Eleni from the Oregon team. Greek Orthodox, icons everywhere. she asked if we're the same church?
options: Close kin: shared sacraments, Mary, icons. Not one communion yet; the pope is the big difference.
Yes, exactly the same church. Only the language and the music are a bit different.
Not really. Orthodox churches don't have sacraments or saints the way Catholics do.
chat.meaning: Catholics and Orthodox share sacraments, bishops, Mary as Theotokos and icons, and are not in full communion, chiefly over the pope's role: both lungs.

Orthodox Churches.meaning: Eastern Churches not in full communion with the pope

Divine Liturgy.meaning: the Eastern name for the Eucharist, the main service

Theotokos.meaning: Greek for God-bearer, a title for Mary

icons.meaning: holy images painted to be prayed with

Nicaea.meaning: a city in today's Turkey where Church councils met

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): shared ground with the Orthodox Churches, in their own words and source (the Divine Liturgy's call before the Creed, paraphrased: 'let us love one another, that with one mind we may confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit'), plus an honest difference (not in full communion; the pope's authority). No ranking, not 'the same'. Please have an Orthodox reader confirm the description is fair. The Filioque difference is not mentioned for length; a Keeper may want it named.
Ut Unum Sint 54 ('the Church must breathe with her two lungs') paraphrased; confirm.
Second Council of Nicaea: 'the honor paid to an image passes to its prototype' (from Basil), paraphrased; confirm.
Married Eastern Catholic priests (CCEO canon 373 and Eastern tradition; some local limits have existed): confirm the phrasing 'by their own tradition'.
The list of Eastern regions (Greece, the Middle East, Russia, Ukraine, Egypt, Ethiopia, India) and 'Catholics recognize so much shared ground' (Unitatis Redintegratio 14–15): confirm.
